sources.citation: Nikulin, Andrey. 2020. Proto-Macro-Jê: um estudo reconstrutivo. Tese de doutorado, Universidade de Brasília. p. 29.
sources.note: Nothing on Sansimoniano prosody. States Sansimoniano is 'uma variedade obviamente relacionada ao Chiquitano.. dispomos de uma curta lista vocabular da mesma da autoria de SNETHLAGE, 1965 [sic, =1935], p. 293', probably extinct, more divergent from modern Chiquitano varieties than they are from each other.
sources.venue: Tese de doutorado, Universidade de Brasília

sources.citation: Snethlage, Rotger Michael. 2002. Life, expeditions, collections and unpublished field notes of Dr. Emil Heinrich Snethlage. In Mily Crevels, Simon van de Kerke, Sérgio Meira & Hein van der Voort (eds.), Current Studies on South American Languages (Indigenous Languages of Latin America [ILLA] 3), 89-102. Leiden: CNWS.
sources.note: No phonology content. Decisive archival statement, section 7 'Scientific diary and word-list' (p. 99-100): 'In my possession are 1.000 pages from the diary-copy and a few vocabularies with about 500 words each from the Pauserna, Kumaná and Abitana-Huanyam, and about 200 words from the Moré. The other lists are lost.' Hence no unpublished Sansimoniano word list survives in the family papers that fed the 2016 Böhlau / 2021 Goeldi diary editions; the 19 forms on ZfE 67: 293 remain the whole corpus. Section 5.14 'Chiquitano' is three sentences on culture loss; the S. Simonianes are not treated se…

sources.note: Nothing. Lists 'San Simoniano - now spoken in the Sierra de San Simón and the Danubio River, Beni province, Bolivia. [E. H. Snethlage 1935, p. 293.]' as a Chiquito dialect and gives ~8 words in a comparative table (some with acute marks, e.g. sóu 'sun', peés 'fire'); no prosodic statement.

sources.citation: Snethlage, Emil Heinrich. 1937. Atiko y: Meine Erlebnisse bei den Indianern des Guaporé. Berlin: Klinkhardt & Biermann.
sources.note: Snethlage's expedition narrative; may repeat or add a few San Simoniano forms; very unlikely to contain prosodic remarks but is the only other first-hand source by the sole recorder.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page 'Sansimoniano' (sans1265) and reference records 143139 (Snethlage 1935) and 18490 (Ramirez 2010).
sources.note: Nothing; classification 'Unclassifiable', AES extinct, both references tagged Glottolog's most extensive description 'a wordlist or less'; no grammar, sketch or phonology reference exists.

sources.citation: Snethlage, Emil Heinrich. 1935 [publ. 1936]. Nachrichten über die Pauserna-Guarayú, die Siriono am Rio Baures und die S. Simonianes in der Nähe der Serra S. Simon. Zeitschrift für Ethnologie 67(5/6): 278-293 (S. Simonianes: pp. 292-293, vocabulary p. 293).
sources.note: No statement on stress, accent or tone anywhere in the article (checked scanned text for Betonung/Akzent/Ton/Aussprache and read pp. 292-293 in full plus the page scan). The only pronunciation remarks are the open-vowel hook and 'consonants as in German'. However the page scan shows that Snethlage wrote an acute accent on almost every S. Simonianes form (natá, wokén, oą́n, njąín, utín, olehín, hokepéin, kabeßín, mänihi [accent on i], topán, päréín, pipín, pökín, sóu, páąn, päú, päí, apá, tabá), i.e. accent MARKS on a 19-item wordlist without any statement of what they denote: wordlist-only pr…

sources.note: Modern specialist treatment that re-examines Snethlage's Sansimoniano list against Chiquitano varieties (per Nikulin 2020:29, includes a phonological analysis of the poorly attested Chiquitano-family varieties); the only modern work likely to comment on the transcription, including any accent marks.

sources.note: The sole primary attestation of Sansimoniano (brief wordlist, p. 293); would show whether Snethlage marked accent on the recorded words and whether he made any remark on pronunciation. Will not contain a stress rule but is the only place any prosodic marking could exist.
